chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Ibn Abi Umayr, from Muawiya ibn Ammar, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said:
The children are carried around (for Tawaf) and stones are thrown on their behalf.
He said, and Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) said: When the woman is sick and does not have full use of her intellect, she is carried around (for Tawaf) or Tawaf is performed on her behalf.

key_terms.لَا تَعْقِلُ: Does not have intellect/cognition (referring to mental state or capacity)
key_terms.يُرْمَى عَنْهُمْ: Stones are thrown on their behalf (referring to Ramy al-Jamarat)
key_terms.يُطَافُ بِهِمْ: They are carried around (passive verb for Tawaf)
key_terms.يُطَافُ عَنْهَا: Tawaf is performed on her behalf

ai.seo_question: How is Tawaf performed for young children and sick individuals who cannot walk or think clearly?
ai.summary: In al-Kafi, Shaykh al-Kulayni records this ruling from Imam al-Sadiq (AS), highlighting the jurisprudential principle of 'Tawaf al-bada'il' (substitute circumambulation) for those excused from performing the ritual themselves. This narration specifically addresses the practical application of this exemption for young children and sick women lacking full cognitive or physical capacity, ensuring their religious obligations are fulfilled through a proxy. It underscores the Shia scholarly emphasis on ease and accessibility in worship, linking physical capability directly to the validity of the act.
